reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
clinicalPearls: Caused most often by a small lacune in the ventral posterolateral or ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus supplied by thalamogeniculate perforators.
Presents with unilateral numbness, tingling or a subjective 'heavy' or 'swollen' sensation of the face, arm, trunk and leg without weakness or cortical signs.
Involvement of all sensory modalities in a hemibody distribution that respects the midline is characteristic of a thalamic lesion.
Objective sensory findings can be strikingly subtle even when symptoms are prominent, so patient-reported distribution is diagnostically valuable.
Dejerine-Roussy thalamic pain syndrome may emerge weeks to months later as delayed, distressing central post-stroke pain in the affected region.
Motor power, visual fields, language and coordination are, by definition, preserved.
MRI with diffusion weighting is far more sensitive than CT for the small thalamic or lemniscal infarct.
Hypertension and diabetes-related small-vessel disease underlie most cases; a cardioembolic or large-artery source should still be excluded.
reference.pathophysiology: Pure sensory stroke arises from occlusion of a small penetrating artery, classically a thalamogeniculate branch of the posterior cerebral artery supplying the ventral posterior thalamic nuclei, the principal relay for the spinothalamic and medial lemniscal pathways. A small lacune here interrupts crossed sensory fibres from the contralateral hemibody while sparing the internal capsule motor fibres, optic radiations and cortex. Less commonly the responsible lesion lies in the lemniscal pathway of the pons or in the parietal white matter. The underlying arteriopathy is typically hypertensive lipohyalinosis or microatheroma of end-arteries, producing the small deep cavity that defines a lacunar infarct.
additionalDifferentials: Sensory seizure or migraine aura with marching paraesthesiae
Cortical parietal infarct causing sensory loss with discriminative features
Multiple sclerosis plaque affecting sensory tracts
additionalInvestigations: Diffusion-weighted and T2/FLAIR MRI focusing on the thalamus and brainstem
Non-contrast CT head to exclude thalamic haemorrhage
ECG and prolonged cardiac rhythm monitoring
HbA1c, fasting glucose and lipid profile
Blood pressure assessment including ambulatory monitoring
redFlags: Reduced consciousness, headache or vomiting suggesting thalamic haemorrhage
Progressive extension of symptoms into motor or cortical domains
Severe delayed central pain heralding thalamic pain syndrome
Bilateral or fluctuating sensory disturbance suggesting an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Sensory symptoms often improve over weeks and the immediate functional outcome is usually favourable, but a minority develop chronic, treatment-resistant central post-stroke (thalamic) pain, and recurrent small-vessel events remain a risk without risk-factor control.
pitfalls: Dismissing prominent subjective numbness as functional because objective signs are minimal.
Missing a small thalamic haemorrhage that can present identically to the ischaemic syndrome.
Failing to warn patients about, or later recognise, delayed thalamic pain.
Relying on an early normal CT and not proceeding to diffusion MRI.
Neglecting embolic-source screening on the assumption of pure small-vessel disease.
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
